content: Patients undergoing tuberculosis (TB) treatment who receive food supplements tend to gain more weight compared to those who do not receive such supplements. However, this weight gain has not been shown to improve TB treatment outcomes. The distribution of macronutrients (protein, carbohydrates, and fats) differs between individuals with active TB and those without the disease. It is generally recommended that all individuals consume approximately 15–30% of their energy from protein, 25–35% from fat, and 45–65% from carbohydrates. Patients with active TB often exhibit low circulating levels of micronutrients, such as vitamins A, E, and D, as well as minerals like iron, zinc, and selenium, at the start of treatment. These levels typically return to normal after two months of appropriate TB therapy. However, it remains unclear whether these deficiencies are due to low dietary intake, altered metabolic processes, or the disease itself. Additionally, it is unknown if the normalization of these levels depends on the quality of dietary intake. Body mass index (BMI) is the most commonly used indicator to assess thinness and fatness in adults over 18 years of age. For children and adolescents aged 5–19 years, BMI-for-age-and-sex Z-scores are used. For children under 5 years, weight-for-length or weight-for-height Z-scores are recommended, with mid-upper arm circumference being used to identify cases requiring life-saving nutritional management. Severe acute malnutrition is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in many settings. Nutritional therapy aims to reduce the risk of death, shorten hospital stays, and facilitate rehabilitation and full recovery. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides recommendations for the definition and treatment of severe acute malnutrition in children, adolescents, and adults. Undernutrition increases the risk of progression from TB infection to active TB disease. Food insecurity and poor nutritional status in populations are major contributors to the global burden of TB. TB diagnosis, treatment, and care often lead to catastrophic health expenditures, worsening food insecurity for patients and their families. TB disproportionately affects individuals aged 15–54 years, who are in their prime working years, exacerbating poverty due to reduced income and increased treatment-related expenses. Pregnant women with TB are at higher risk of complications, including pre-eclampsia, and their infants are more likely to have low birth weight, premature birth, or perinatal death. Adequate weight gain during pregnancy is crucial for improving birth outcomes. Calcium supplementation is recommended in populations with low calcium intake to prevent pre-eclampsia. Micronutrient requirements during pregnancy are generally 25–50% higher than pre-pregnancy levels. While no randomized controlled trials have been conducted on micronutrient supplementation in pregnant women with TB, studies in non-HIV-infected populations have shown that multiple micronutrient supplements can reduce rates of low birth weight, small-for-gestational-age infants, and anemia. Children in households with TB patients are at increased risk of infection due to close contact. Undernourished children and those with immature immune systems are particularly vulnerable. Screening household contacts for TB can help detect the disease early, but this is often not prioritized in lowto middle-income countries. Malnourished children may fail to mount an immune response to TB skin tests, increasing the likelihood of missed diagnoses. Improved nutrition among household contacts, especially children under 10 years of age, may reduce the risk of developing active TB. The WHO guideline on nutritional care and support for TB patients was developed following evidence-informed procedures. Advisory groups, including the WHO Steering Committee for Nutrition Guidelines Development and the Nutrition Guidance Advisory Group, were established to guide the process. The guideline development involved consultations with external experts and stakeholders, evidence appraisal using the GRADE approach, and systematic reviews. Recommendations were formulated based on available evidence and previous WHO guidance on nutritional care and support.
